subject: Geography B
title: GCSE (9-1) Geography B
sourceNote: Pearson Edexcel Level 1/Level 2 GCSE (9-1) Geography B specification, Issue 4, September 2025: the copy of Pearson's published PDF captured by the Internet Archive on 2026-05-13 (qualifications.pearson.com could not be reached directly from the build environment).
notes: Numbering: Pearson numbers each key idea within its topic (1.1 ... 9.6) and letters the detailed content beneath it (1.1a, 1.1b). Enquiry questions are printed but not numbered. Key ideas are the leaf points (refs); the lettered detail and the numbered integrated skills are not separate refs.

One topic = one pack. Geography B has no optional units: Topic 4's sub-topics 4A Coastal change and conflict and 4B River processes and pressures are both compulsory, so they are subtopics of Topic 4.

Subtopics have registry refs (<topic>.g<n>): one per enquiry question, split where an enquiry question covers very different key ideas, with short titles written for the registry (the enquiry question is in the text file). parents maps each key idea to its subtopic.
Topics 7–9 (Component 3, People and environment issues) are kept as content; the decision-making exam (Paper 3) uses a resource booklet given out in the exam, not a pre-release.

Skipped: Topic 6 Geographical investigations (fieldwork and research, school-dependent), and the separate Geographical skills section (skills are listed with each key idea in the text files but are not refs).

subtopics.title: Global climate system and climate change
Quality of life in a megacity
Overview of the UK’s physical landscape
Overview of the UK’s human landscape
Case study: a major UK city
Case study: the city’s rural area
The biosphere as a life-support system

refs.1.1: The atmosphere operates as a global system which transfers heat around the Earth
refs.1.2: Climate has changed in the past through natural causes on timescales ranging from hundreds to millions of years
refs.1.3: Global climate is now changing as a result of human activity, and there is uncertainty about future climates
refs.1.4: Tropical cyclones are caused by particular meteorological conditions
refs.1.5: Tropical cyclones present major natural hazards to people and places
refs.1.6: The impacts of tropical cyclones are linked to a country’s ability to prepare and respond to them
refs.1.7: Earth’s layered structure, and physical properties is key to plate tectonics
refs.1.8: There are different plate boundaries, each with characteristic volcanic and earthquake hazards
refs.1.9: Tectonic hazards affect people, and are managed, differently at contrasting locations
refs.2.1: There are different ways of defining and measuring development
refs.2.2: There is global inequality in development and different theories in how it can be reduced
refs.2.3: Approaches to development vary in type and success
refs.2.4: Development of the emerging country is influenced by its location and context in the world
refs.2.5: Globalisation causes rapid economic change in the emerging country
refs.2.6: Rapid economic growth results in significant positive and negative impacts on people and environment in the emerging country
refs.2.7: Rapid economic development has changed the international role of the emerging country
refs.3.1: The world is becoming increasingly urbanised
refs.3.2: Urbanisation is a result of socio-economic processes and change
refs.3.3: Cities change over time and this is reflected in changing land use
refs.3.4: The location and context of the chosen megacity influences its growth, function and structure
refs.3.5: The megacity in the chosen country is growing rapidly
refs.3.6: Rapid population growth creates opportunities and challenges for people living in the chosen megacity
refs.3.7: Quality of life in the chosen megacity can be improved by different strategies for achieving sustainability
refs.4.1: Geology and past processes have influenced the physical landscape of the UK
refs.4.2: A number of physical and human processes work together to create distinct UK landscapes
refs.4.3: Distinctive coastal landscapes are influenced by geology interacting with physical processes
refs.4.4: Distinctive coastal landscapes are modified by human activity interacting with physical processes
refs.4.5: The interaction of human and physical processes present challenges along coastlines and there are a variety of management options
refs.4.6: Distinctive river landscapes have different characteristics formed by interacting physical processes
refs.4.7: River landscapes are influenced by human activity interacting with physical processes
refs.4.8: Some rivers are more prone to flood than others and there is a variety of river management options
refs.5.1: Population, economic activities and settlements are key elements of the human landscape
refs.5.2: The UK economy and society is increasingly linked and shaped by the wider world
refs.5.3: The context of the city influences its functions and structure
refs.5.4: The city changes through employment, services and the movement of people
refs.5.5: The changing city creates challenges and opportunities
refs.5.6: Ways of life in the city can be improved by different strategies
refs.5.7: The city is interdependent with rural areas, leading to changes in rural areas
refs.5.8: The changing rural area creates challenges and opportunities
refs.7.1: The Earth is home to a number of very large ecosystems (biomes) the distribution of which is affected by climate and other factors
refs.7.2: The biosphere is a vital life-support system for people as it provides both goods and services
refs.8.1: The structure, functioning and adaptations of the tropical rainforest* reflect the equatorial climate
refs.8.2: The taiga shows different characteristics, reflecting the more extreme and highly seasonal climate
refs.8.3: Tropical rainforests are threatened directly by deforestation and indirectly by climate change
refs.8.4: The taiga is increasingly threatened by commercial development
refs.8.5: Conservation and sustainable management of tropical rain forests is vital if goods and services are not to be lost for future generations
refs.8.6: The taiga wilderness areas need to be protected from over-exploitation
refs.9.1: Energy resources can be classified in different ways and their extraction and use has environmental consequences
refs.9.2: Access to energy resources is not evenly distributed which has implications for people
refs.9.3: The global demand for oil is increasing, but supplies are unevenly available
refs.9.4: The world’s continuing reliance of fossil fuels increases pressure to exploit new areas
refs.9.5: Reducing reliance on fossil fuels presents major technical challenges
refs.9.6: Attitudes to energy and environmental issues are changing
